docs.title: 🗺️ Learning Roadmap
docs.text:
Ten sections — each building directly on the last. Start at Section 1 and work your way through.

🧱 1 · Python Basics & Syntax Variables, data types, operators, OOP, file handling, and your first Flask API. Lessons 1–10 · Beginner

🗃️ 2 · Databases, ORMs & Auth SQLite, SQLAlchemy, MongoDB, Flask auth, JWT tokens, and FastAPI CRUD. Lessons 11–20 · Beginner+

🌐 3 · Real-World API Projects Build a weather app, URL shortener, news aggregator, email service, and more. Lessons 21–30 · Intermediate

⚙️ 4 · Async, CI/CD & Docker asyncio, Celery, Redis caching, Pytest, GitHub Actions CI, and Docker. Lessons 31–40 · Intermediate

🔒 5 · Security & Microservices OAuth2, webhooks, RabbitMQ, Redis Pub/Sub, load testing, and API gateways. Lessons 41–50 · Intermediate+

🖥️ 6 · Frontend Integrations Streamlit, React, Jinja2 templates, AJAX, and building full-stack dashboards. Lessons 51–60 · Intermediate

📊 7 · Data APIs & Visualization Pandas APIs, CSV/JSON exports, Matplotlib, Plotly Dash, and data pipelines. Lessons 61–70 · Intermediate+

☁️ 8 · Cloud & Serverless AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure, WebSockets, GraphQL, and payments. Lessons 71–80 · Advanced

🧠 9 · Machine Learning & AI Scikit-Learn APIs, NLP sentiment, image classification, chatbots, and MLOps. Lessons 81–90 · Advanced

🏢 10 · Enterprise Architecture Multi-tenancy, RBAC, observability, scalable deployment, and your capstone project. Lessons 91–100 · Expert

docs.text:
🧱 Basics → 🗃️ Databases → 🌐 APIs → ⚙️ Async & CI/CD → 🔒 Security

Practice Python for Beginners is a free, open-source learning platform designed to take you from your very first line of Python to building production-grade enterprise applications — all through hands-on practice.

docs.title: 📖 Introduction
docs.text:
Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world — used everywhere from web development and data science to machine learning and automation. One reason for its popularity is its readable, English-like syntax.

Let's start at the very beginning.

No installation needed

Every code block on this page has a ▶ Run button. Click it to execute Python directly in your browser — no setup required!

docs.title: 1. Variables & Assignment
docs.text:
A variable is a named container that holds a value. In Python you create a variable simply by assigning a value to it — no var, let, or type declaration needed.

# This is a comment — Python ignores everything after #

name = "Alice"       # str  (text)
age  = 25            # int  (whole number)
height = 1.68        # float (decimal)
is_student = True    # bool (True or False)
nothing = None       # NoneType (absence of value)

print(name, age, height, is_student, nothing)

Naming conventions

Use snake_case for variable names (user_name, not UserName or userName). Names are case-sensitive: age, Age, and AGE are three different variables.

Try it yourself — change the values and hit Run:

name = "Alice"
age  = 25
height = 1.68
is_student = True

print(f"Name: {name}")
print(f"Age: {age}")
print(f"Height: {height}m")
print(f"Is a student: {is_student}")

docs.title: 2. Built-in Data Types
docs.text:
Python has several built-in data types. Here are the ones you'll use most often:

StringsNumbersBooleansType Conversion 

# Strings — text wrapped in quotes (single or double)
greeting = "Hello, World!"
language = 'Python'

# Multi-line strings use triple quotes
bio = """
My name is Alice.
I am learning Python.
"""

print(greeting)
print(language)
print(bio)

Hello, World!
Python

My name is Alice.
I am learning Python.


# int — whole numbers (no decimal point)
apples = 5
temperature = -3

# float — numbers with a decimal point
pi = 3.14159
price = 9.99

print(type(apples))       # <class 'int'>
print(type(pi))           # <class 'float'>
print(apples + pi)        # 8.14159

<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
8.14159


# bool — either True or False (capital T and F!)
is_raining = False
has_umbrella = True

# Booleans are the result of comparisons
print(5 > 3)          # True
print(10 == 20)       # False
print(is_raining and has_umbrella)  # False

True
False
False


# Convert between types with int(), float(), str(), bool()
x = "42"          # This is a string "42"
y = int(x)        # Now it's the integer 42
z = float(y)      # Now it's 42.0

print(type(x), x)   # <class 'str'>  42
print(type(y), y)   # <class 'int'>  42
print(type(z), z)   # <class 'float'> 42.0

# Check the type of any value
print(isinstance(y, int))   # True

<class 'str'> 42
<class 'int'> 42
<class 'float'> 42.0
True

docs.title: Comparison Operators
docs.text:
x = 10
print(x == 10)   # True  — equal to
print(x != 5)    # True  — not equal to
print(x > 7)     # True  — greater than
print(x < 7)     # False — less than
print(x >= 10)   # True  — greater than or equal
print(x <= 9)    # False — less than or equal

docs.title: Logical Operators
docs.text:
a = True
b = False

print(a and b)   # False — both must be True
print(a or b)    # True  — at least one must be True
print(not a)     # False — flips the boolean

Common mistake: = vs ==

= assigns a value. == compares two values. 

x = 5      # ✅ assignment
x == 5     # ✅ comparison (returns True)
if x = 5:  # ❌ SyntaxError!

docs.title: 4. print() and input()
docs.text:
print() outputs values to the screen. input() pauses and waits for the user to type something.

PythonOutput 
# print() can take multiple values separated by commas
print("Hello", "World", 42)

# sep changes the separator (default is a space)
print("2024", "01", "15", sep="-")

# end changes what's printed at the end (default is newline \n)
print("Loading", end="")
print("...", end="\n")

# f-strings are the modern way to embed variables
name = "Bob"
score = 97.5
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}%")

Hello World 42
2024-01-15
Loading...
Bob scored 97.5%

input() in the browser runner

The live runner on this page uses Pyodide (Python in WebAssembly). The input() function is not supported in the browser environment. For input() examples, run them locally with python script.py in your terminal.

docs.title: 5. Conditional Statements (if / elif / else)
docs.text:
Conditionals let your program make decisions.

PythonOutput 
score = 78

if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "D"
else:
    grade = "F"

print(f"Score: {score} → Grade: {grade}")

Score: 78 → Grade: C

Indentation is not optional

Python uses indentation (4 spaces) to define code blocks — there are no { } braces. Every line inside an if block must be indented consistently. 

if True:
    print("This works")   # ✅
  print("This breaks")    # ❌ IndentationError

Try it — change the value of score and re-run:

score = 78   # ← change this value and click Run

if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "D"
else:
    grade = "F"

print(f"Score: {score} → Grade: {grade}")

docs.title: 6. Common Beginner Mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Using a variable before assigning it 
print(result)   # ❌ NameError: name 'result' is not defined
result = 42
print(result)   # ✅
Mistake 2: Wrong indentation 
for i in range(3):
print(i)   # ❌ IndentationError — must be indented
    print(i)  # ✅
Mistake 3: Comparing strings with wrong case 
answer = input("Yes or No? ")
if answer == "yes":    # ❌ won't match "Yes" or "YES"
    print("Great!")

if answer.lower() == "yes":   # ✅ case-insensitive
    print("Great!")
Mistake 4: Integer division when float expected 
print(7 / 2)    # 3.5  ✅
print(7 // 2)   # 3    (floor division — may not be what you want)
